reason: This passage (2 Samuel 11-12) presents a cautionary narrative of leadership failure rather than a model of good leadership. King David exhibits the opposite of responsible accountability: he abdicates his duty by remaining in Jerusalem while his army fights (11:1), commits adultery with Bathsheba, and orchestrates the death of her husband Uriah to conceal his sin (11:14-17). While David eventually repents when confronted by the prophet Nathan ('I have sinned against the Lord,' 12:13), this is reactive repentance only after direct confrontation, not proactive responsibility for his people's welfare. The passage emphasizes the grave consequences of his failure—the death of his child and the Lord's judgment that 'the sword will not depart from your house' (12:10)—which underscore how fundamentally David violated his responsibilities as a leader accountable for his people.
